title: Black Robin, Condor, Bison: Back From Almost Zero. #1 Had 5 Left
description: A new study (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Nov 2026) checked every bird and mammal that fell below 50 animals since 1950: with active help, 61% recovered to 100+, without it only 2%. We count down five comebacks, from the Lord Howe woodhen and the California condor to the European bison, the Mauritius kestrel, and #1: the black robin, saved by one mother called Old Blue. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: In 1980, this bird was down to five. Not five thousand. Five birds on Earth.

scenes.label: 1 breeding female
scenes.say: And only one of them could still lay eggs. One mother, holding a whole species on her back.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: So how is it still alive today? That story is number one, and it's the craziest rescue I've ever read.

scenes.label: 'Too few to save'
scenes.say: Because here's the thing. For decades, scientists believed that once an animal drops that low, it's basically finished.
Too few animals means too much inbreeding, and the population slowly collapses. Game over. That was the idea.

scenes.label: Study: Nov 2026
scenes.say: But a brand new study, published this week, checked every bird and mammal that fell under fifty since 1950.
And the answer surprised a lot of people. So today, five animals that came back from almost zero. Each one closer to the edge.

scenes.label: Lord Howe woodhen
scenes.say: Number five. A brown bird that can't fly, living on one tiny island that belongs to Australia.

scenes.label: Humans arrive, 1788
scenes.say: This is Lord Howe Island. People arrived in 1788, and they brought pigs, cats, and rats with them.
Okay, so think about that from the bird's side. It can't fly. And suddenly everything wants to eat it or its eggs.

scenes.label: Only 23 left
scenes.say: By the late 1970s, scientists estimated just 23 woodhens were left. Twenty-three birds. That's one classroom.

scenes.label: Pigs and cats out
scenes.say: So the rescue team did two things. First, they removed the feral pigs and cats that were wrecking the island.

scenes.label: Bred, then released
scenes.say: Second, starting in 1980, they bred woodhens in captivity for four years, then let them go.

scenes.label: Stuck at ~200
scenes.say: It worked. But the population got stuck around two hundred birds. For almost forty years. Something was still holding them back.

scenes.label: Rats removed, 2019
scenes.say: That something was rats. In 2019, the island got rid of its rats. And during the poison bait drop, the woodhens were kept safe in care.
Then they were released into a rat-free island. And by 2024? There were 1,638 woodhens.
From 23 to over sixteen hundred. And that's only number five. Because the next animal wasn't just rare. It vanished from the sky.

scenes.label: 9.5 ft wings
scenes.say: Number four. The California condor. North America's biggest land bird, with wings about nine and a half feet across.

scenes.label: 22 in the wild
scenes.say: These giants once flew over a huge part of the continent. But by 1982, only 22 were left in the wild.

scenes.label: Catch them all?
scenes.say: So scientists made a decision that people fought about for years. Catch every last one.

scenes.label: April 1987
scenes.say: In April 1987, the last wild condor was captured. It was a bird called AC9. And at that moment, no condor flew free anywhere.

scenes.label: 27 on Earth
scenes.say: The entire species was now 27 birds, living in two zoos in California. That's it. Twenty-seven.

scenes.label: Back in the sky, 1992
scenes.say: Then, in 1992, the first two zoo-raised condors were released. Slowly, the numbers climbed.

scenes.label: Wild chicks again
scenes.say: Today they glide over Big Sur, the Grand Canyon, and even Mexico. Some have hatched chicks in the wild.
By the end of 2025, there were 607 condors. And 392 of them were flying free.

scenes.label: The hidden killer
scenes.say: But here's the twist. The biggest killer of wild condors isn't old age. It's lead.

scenes.label: Lead poisoning
scenes.say: Condors eat dead animals. If that animal was shot with lead bullets, the condor swallows the fragments.

scenes.label: ~49% of known deaths
scenes.say: From 1992 to 2024, lead poisoning caused about half of the known condor deaths in the wild. So the rescue isn't finished.
Still, from 27 to over six hundred. But what if an animal hit zero in the wild? Not 22. Zero. That's number three.

scenes.label: Europe's giant
scenes.say: Number three. The European bison. The heaviest land animal in Europe.

scenes.label: France to the Volga
scenes.say: Long ago, they roamed from France all the way to Russia. Then hunting and farming squeezed them into a few forests.

scenes.label: Białowieża Forest
scenes.say: The last big stronghold was this ancient forest between Poland and Belarus. Then World War One came through it.
Soldiers and poachers hunted them. In 1919, the last wild bison in this forest was killed.

scenes.label: Extinct in the wild, 1927
scenes.say: A few still hid in the Caucasus Mountains. In 1927, the very last one there was shot too. Extinct in the wild.

scenes.label: 54 in zoos
scenes.say: So what was left? Animals in zoos and private parks. In 1924, the whole species was just 54 bison.

scenes.label: 12 founders
scenes.say: And here's the scary part. Every European bison alive today comes from just 12 of those animals. Twelve.
That's like rebuilding a whole country from twelve people. Scientists were worried about that for a hundred years.

scenes.label: Return, 1952
scenes.say: In 1952, the first zoo-born bison walked back into that same forest. And they kept going.
By 2020, there were 9,111 European bison, and 6,819 of them lived free in 47 herds.
Okay, quick question for you. Which comeback is bigger so far? Drop a five, four, or three in the comments.
Because the next one was officially called hopeless. In writing. By experts.

scenes.label: Mauritius kestrel
scenes.say: Number two. The Mauritius kestrel. A small falcon that lives in the forests of one island in the Indian Ocean.

scenes.label: 4 wild birds
scenes.say: Invasive animals, cut-down forests, and pesticides hit it hard. By 1974, only four were left in the wild.

scenes.label: 'Virtually nil'
scenes.say: Four. Experts at the time wrote that its chances in the wild seemed 'virtually nil'.

scenes.label: 'Abandon it'
scenes.say: One even suggested it might be better to abandon it and spend the money on other birds.
But a team refused. They controlled predators, put out extra food, and built safe nest sites.
Teams also moved eggs between nests and raised birds in care, then sent them back to the forest.

scenes.label: 4 → up to 500
scenes.say: And it worked. By the late 1990s, there were somewhere between 350 and 500 kestrels.

scenes.label: Also 'doomed'
scenes.say: Two other 'doomed' birds on the same island, the pink pigeon and the echo parakeet, now number in the hundreds too.

scenes.label: 3 out of 3
scenes.say: That's three species on one island that experts had basically written off. All three are still flying today.

scenes.label: Under 250, 2021
scenes.say: But I promised you honest stories. The kestrel has dropped again, to under 250 in 2021. It still needs help.
Still, four birds. Most people would have given up. And number one had even less to work with.

scenes.label: Black robin
scenes.say: Number one. The Chatham Island black robin. A tiny, all-black bird that weighs only about 22 to 25 grams.

scenes.label: 800 km offshore
scenes.say: It lives on remote islands about 800 kilometers off New Zealand. Cats and rats wiped it out almost everywhere.

scenes.label: 5 birds. 1 pair
scenes.say: By the end of the 1979 season, only five black robins were alive. Just one breeding pair, Old Blue and Old Yellow.

scenes.label: Old Blue
scenes.say: Old Blue was the only female who could still breed. Every future black robin depended on her.

scenes.label: ~4-year lifespan
scenes.say: And time was running out. On average, a black robin only lives about four years.

scenes.label: The egg swap
scenes.say: So a team led by Don Merton tried a wild trick. They took her eggs and slipped them into another bird's nest.

scenes.label: One brood a year
scenes.say: Here's why that's genius. A black robin pair normally raises just one set of chicks a season. That's painfully slow.

scenes.label: Foster parents
scenes.say: These tomtits didn't notice. They raised the robin chicks like their own babies.

scenes.label: 3 clutches
scenes.say: And Old Blue? She had lost her eggs, so she laid more. In one season, she laid three clutches instead of one.
By 1982, there were 12 robins. Every single chick came from Old Blue and Old Yellow.

scenes.label: 100+ by 1989
scenes.say: By 1989, over 100. Old Blue lived to about 14, more than twice a normal robin's life.

scenes.label: All from Old Blue
scenes.say: And here's the part that blows my mind. Every black robin alive today descends from that one bird.

scenes.label: Inbreeding? Not yet
scenes.say: Scientists expected inbreeding to finish them. But so far, it doesn't seem to have caused big problems.

scenes.label: 1 mother → 445
scenes.say: In 2025, New Zealand's conservation department counted about 445 black robins. From one mother.

scenes.label: 141 species
scenes.say: So, back to that new study. It looked at 141 species that fell below fifty animals. Birds and mammals, all over the world.

scenes.label: 61% vs 2%
scenes.say: When people actively helped, 61 percent climbed back to at least a hundred. Without help? Only 2 percent did.

scenes.label: Vaquita: ~10
scenes.say: And over a third of the species nobody helped went extinct. Right now, the vaquita porpoise is down to about ten animals.

scenes.label: Comment below
scenes.say: So is any animal ever too few to save? Old Blue says no. Comment below: which comeback should I cover next?

short.title: 5 Birds Left on Earth. One Mother Saved Them All
short.header: The bird saved by one mother
short.description: In 1980 only five black robins were left, with one breeding female: Old Blue. Scientists swapped her eggs into tomtit nests, and today about 445 robins (NZ DOC, 2025) all descend from her. Full countdown of 5 comebacks on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Five birds left on Earth, and only one mother. This is how she saved them.
In 1980, the Chatham Island black robin was down to five birds. Only one female could still breed. Her name was Old Blue.

scenes.label: The egg swap
scenes.say: So scientists stole her eggs and hid them in a tomtit's nest. The tomtits raised the chicks like their own.

scenes.label: 3 clutches
scenes.say: And Old Blue, missing her eggs, just laid more. Three sets of eggs in one single season.

scenes.label: 100+ by 1989
scenes.say: By 1989 there were over a hundred robins. And Old Blue lived to fourteen, more than twice a normal robin's life.

scenes.label: ~445 today
scenes.say: Today there are about 445, and every single one is her descendant. All from one bird, because once there were only
